issues.legal_issue: Taking cognizance of an offence and issuing process to an accused are distinct stages of a criminal proceeding.
material_facts: A police report was filed in the criminal case, and the Magistrate later summoned the accused.
The Court considered the respective functions of taking cognizance and issuing process under the Code.
issues.conclusion: Taking cognizance is distinct from issuing process: cognizance is the Magistrate’s judicial notice of an offence, while process may be issued when there is sufficient ground for proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 190 and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, cognizance is the application of judicial mind to the alleged offence and is taken of cases, not persons. It is a condition precedent to initiating proceedings, while issuing process is a subsequent step requiring sufficient ground for proceeding, not sufficient ground for conviction. The Court relied on S.K. Sinha, Chief Enforcement Officer v. Videocon International Ltd. (2008) 2 SCC 492.

predicates.magistrate_criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case before a Magistrate.
predicates.magistrate_takes_judicial_notice_of_offe: The Magistrate applies judicial mind to the alleged offence and takes notice of it.
predicates.sufficient_ground_for_proceeding: The Magistrate forms the opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against an accused.

issues.definition: When a Magistrate in a criminal proceeding takes judicial notice of an offence and finds sufficient ground to proceed, taking cognizance and issuing process remain distinct stages.

issues.legal_issue: A Magistrate issuing process need not expressly state reasons in the order, provided the Magistrate forms the opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding.
material_facts: The Magistrate summoned the accused after a police report and accompanying materials had been filed.
The summoning order did not set out express reasons.
The challenge to the order included the absence of reasons as a ground for setting it aside.
issues.conclusion: The summoning order could not be faulted solely because it did not state express reasons.
issues.legal_principle: Section 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 requires the Magistrate to form an opinion that sufficient ground for proceeding exists, but does not require an express narration of reasons in an order issuing process. At this stage, the question is whether there is sufficient ground to proceed, not whether there is sufficient ground for conviction. The Court relied on Kanti Bhadra Shah v. State of West Bengal (2000) 1 SCC 722; Smt. Nagawwa v. Veeranna Shivalingappa Konjalgi (1976) 3 SCC 736; Dy. Chief Controller of Imports & Exports v. Roshanlal Agarwal (2003) 4 SCC 139; U.P. Pollution Control Board v. Mohan Meakins Ltd. (2000) 3 SCC 745; and U.P. Pollution Control Board v. Dr. Bhupendra Kumar Modi (2009) 2 SCC 147.

predicates.magistrate_criminal_process: The matter is a criminal proceeding in which a Magistrate considers issuing process.
predicates.magistrate_issues_process: The Magistrate issues process against an accused after forming the required opinion that there is sufficient ground to proceed.
predicates.process_order_lacks_explicit_reasons: The order issuing process does not expressly set out the Magistrate’s reasons.

issues.definition: When a Magistrate issues process in a criminal proceeding and the order lacks express reasons, that omission alone does not invalidate the process.

issues.legal_issue: A petition invoking the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction to challenge a summoning order is maintainable.
material_facts: The accused petitioned the High Court under Section 482 of the Code to challenge the Magistrate’s summoning order.
The High Court concluded that the petition was not maintainable.
The Supreme Court rejected that conclusion while confirming the High Court’s decision on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The petition under Section 482 was maintainable, although the appeals were dismissed and the High Court’s order was confirmed on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court’s inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 may be invoked to challenge criminal proceedings, including a summoning order. The Court relied on Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Special Judicial Magistrate (1998) 5 SCC 749; Dhariwal Tobacco Products Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2009) 2 SCC 370; and M.A.A. Annamalai v. State of Karnataka (2010) 8 SCC 524.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter arises from a criminal proceeding.
predicates.petition_invokes_high_court_inherent_jur: A petition asks the High Court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction.
predicates.petition_challenges_summoning_order: The petition challenges an order summoning an accused to appear.

issues.definition: A petition invoking the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction to challenge a summoning order in a criminal proceeding is maintainable.
